headline: Still the most-owned stock on eToro platform; long-term core holding, expected to remain so for a long time
reasoning: Gilbert described Nvidia as a long-term core holding and the most owned stock on the eToro platform. Despite near-term volatility from AI safety debates and rate hikes, the fundamental demand for AI chips has not changed. He indicated this positioning is unlikely to shift in the foreseeable future.
quote: That AI trade still remains the center, still got Nvidia is that sort of long term core holding, still the most owned stock on the platform, and I think will be for a long time to come.

headline: AI investment cycle still in early stages; pausing for review is not a reason to exit the theme, but monitor Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon capex signals and chip order trends closely
reasoning: Gilbert argued that the capital committed to AI infrastructure build-out is already in the system and the underlying demand for processors, memory, networking, cooling and power remains intact. The real risk signal would be hyperscalers cutting capex, chip orders softening, or hard government restrictions on model training — none of which appear imminent. He views the recent volatility as a temporary pause, not the end of the AI investment cycle.
quote: I think if we look at the money that's behind this build out, a lot of it's been committed already. So the idea for running them and sort of also need to deliver them, we still need processors, memory, networking, calling, and an enormous amount of power... what would really be the concerning side of this is if we start to see your Microsoft, your alphabets, Amazons, etc., if we start to hear from them cutting capital spending or pulling back, or start to see chip orders soften... I think the base case here is a temporary rise in volatility, certainly not the end to this investment cycle.

headline: Higher for longer a positive outcome for Australian bank lenders; capital flowing into banks and industrials as rate hike boosted net interest margin outlook
reasoning: Gilbert explained that Australian banks outperformed on the day because higher-for-longer interest rates are a favourable environment for lenders. He noted significant capital flows into banks and industrials, with NAB leading gains. The out-of-cycle rate hikes by ANZ and NAB further reinforced the sector's earnings tailwind.
quote: A big part of the good news obviously came from the fact that we had banks higher today. We saw a lot of capital flowing into banks and industrials, as you said, a minute ago, nabbed up pretty well today. Higher for longer is a perfectly good outcome if you're a lender.

headline: Fed hike was largely priced in but the hawkishness surprised; another hike signalled before year-end via dot plot (16 of 18 FOMC members), rates at 4% with higher-for-longer now the base case
reasoning: Josh Gilbert noted the Fed hike itself was mostly priced in but the degree of hawkishness was unexpected. The dot plot showed 16 of 18 Fed members projecting another hike before year-end. Rates sitting at 4% represent a dramatic shift from the start of the year when cuts were seen as more likely. This raises borrowing costs for hyperscalers and broadly changes the investment calculus for risk assets.
quote: The hike itself was mainly priced in, but the hawkishness I don't think we would have expected so much. We've also got an ultra-Hawkish Fed now, right? The decision made through today, unanimous. And that's a long way from where we were at the start of the year. We also saw the dot plot coming through today, 16 out of the 18, putting through new projections, looking for another hike before the year is out.

headline: Bitcoin thesis intact despite Clarity Act setback; capital rotation to AI has constrained crypto flows, but trading activity picks up sharply on price moves from 59-60k to ~80k
reasoning: Gilbert noted the failure to pass the Clarity Act was a short-term headwind for crypto but did not fundamentally change the investment thesis for Bitcoin. The bigger constraint on crypto has been competition for capital from the AI trade, which has delivered strong returns. He observed that trading activity on eToro picked up significantly during the recent move from around $59-60k to near $80k.
quote: I don't think for me, though, that sort of clarity act changed anything too much in the short term, I think the theses behind, you know, Bitcoin is sort of still there... it's just been a really tough time for capital to flow to crypto assets when we've had such a booming run that we've seen, you know, in AI and, you know, the returns that we're seeing from, you know, those assets. Whenever we see, you know, a move that we have done in sort of the last month or so, where we went from sort of the lows of 59 to 60 thousand to pushing to 80, we certainly do see trading activity sort of pick up around those crypto assets.

headline: Higher rates, oil above $100, and persistent inflation make this a difficult balancing act for investors, but strong US earnings season keeps the bull case alive
reasoning: Gilbert acknowledged the challenging combination of higher interest rates, oil prices back above $100, and sticky inflation globally. Despite these headwinds, US earnings season was strong and growth continues, which supports current market levels. He emphasised that there is always something to worry about but markets historically reward staying invested rather than sitting on the sidelines.
quote: I think when you have the combination of higher rates that we're getting at the moment, oil prices where they are, inflation still proving to be really, really difficult globally for central banks to sort of fight, it does make a difficult position... when we look at sort of what we just had from earning season in the US, it was fantastic. And we're obviously still seeing that growth coming through too. So there is a balancing act here, and I think it's a really difficult one to balance.

headline: Shares up ~20% YTD trading at ~35x forward earnings; high expectations leave little room for disappointment ahead of first major product event under new CEO John Ternus
reasoning: Josh Gilbert notes that historically Apple shares have fallen into its iPhone launch events and continued falling after in three of the last five events, suggesting the market has repeatedly been unimpressed. Last year was an exception with the iPhone 17 launch. Shares are currently up about 20% for the year and trade at approximately 35 times forward earnings, reflecting elevated expectations. Gilbert sees the appointment of hardware engineer Ternus as a signal of a strategic shift back toward device innovation after Tim Cook's 15-year focus on building out services. The key catalyst to watch is whether a revamped Siri AI can function as an agent — executing tasks across third-party apps like WhatsApp and Amazon Alexa — which requires cooperation from companies like Meta and Amazon, making this less an Apple-only challenge and more a third-party integration question.
quote: Yeah. And I think that's the, the key point. If we look back at sort of the, the sort of the, the iPhone launch events in the past coming into them for the last five shares have actually fallen coming into the event and, and in three of those they've sort of kept falling afterwards. So firstly, I think it tells us the market, you know, hasn't been expecting much in the past and then hasn't been impressed with what's come up as well. Last year was different when we, we had the launch of the iPhone 17, the, the, you know, the market was upcoming into the event and then was up after the event as well. So history hasn't been kind to it. But I think there's a lot of expectation coming in. Shares are up about 20% this year, trading at about 35 times forward earnings. You know, so that's the market telling us they're expecting a lot and you know, they're paying a premium for it at the same time. So that leaves very little room for disappointment.
episode_title: New products herald Apple's Ternus turn

headline: Josh Gilbert says CSL gave the market what it needed to hear on restructuring and growth path despite a torrid couple of years
reasoning: CSL has struggled for a couple of years but presented a restructuring plan and outlined a growth pathway that was better than market expectations. Gilbert indicated the result itself wasn't necessarily strong but the communication around next year laying the groundwork for recovery was reassuring. He cautioned it doesn't mean performance will immediately improve but market reception was positive.
quote: If we think about ASX and if we think about CSL, two companies that have been really struggling but sort of gave the market what it wanted to hear in terms of restructuring plans, you know, the next leg of growth. I think CSL was a great example. A torrid couple of years, but sort of really laid out that it had been a difficult period. Next year was going to be sort of the year where it starts to lay the groundwork back to its best. I don't think what we heard from them was meaning that it's going to be better, but it was better than what I think the market was anticipating.

headline: Josh Gilbert argues Qantas's 14% profit decline was a fuel-shock story rather than a business problem, with underlying resilience from Jetstar and loyalty segments
reasoning: Underlying profit fell 14% primarily due to higher fuel costs from Middle East conflict rather than structural business weakness. Jetstar's domestic operations and the loyalty business performed well, while international earnings fell ~40% due to fuel costs and ageing fleet. Qantas is raising fares while reducing seats, relying on its duopoly position with Virgin, but Gilbert flags risk that consumers may push back as cost-of-living pressures intensify. He views fuel shocks as temporary and notes oil prices have already begun to ease.
quote: Yes, profits did fall 14 percent. But most of that actually came from a big hit from higher fuel costs and what we've obviously been seeing in the Middle East. So that impact was mainly a fuel shock doing the damage rather than a business problem, ultimately. And I think it showed us that overall, it was a pretty resilient result in what was a pretty difficult year. Some real strength coming through from Jetstar domestically and also its loyalty business as well... The question is just how long passengers will keep taking the brunt of that? Because ultimately, we know the rate rises that we've seen. Another rate rise on the table. Our wallets aren't bottomless. And we're already starting to see that planes are flying a little empty already.

headline: Josh Gilbert sees Nvidia's massive revenue result as supply-constrained rather than demand-limited, with AI agent expansion set to drive further compute growth
reasoning: Nvidia revenue more than doubled to close to $100 billion, with guidance of ~$108 billion for the next quarter exceeding market expectations. Jensen Huang noted demand is running at close to 100% growth but Nvidia can only supply around 70% due to physical constraints, meaning this is a supply problem, not a demand problem. The shift from AI 'thinking' to AI 'doing' (agents) will require significantly more compute per query, underpinning a multi-year demand runway. Gilbert also noted that hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are already seeing AI capex pay off through earnings, validating continued investment.
quote: Revenue more than doubled to close to $100 billion. Ultimately making nearly a billion dollars a day in revenue, which is pretty eye watering. The data center business is again still that sort of key driver and its guidance the next quarter was also strong, you know, around about $108 billion as well. And that was more than what the market wanted... Jensen essentially saying the demand is running close to 100 percent growth. But then Nvidia is only going to commit to about 70 percent because that's all it can physically supply. So this isn't, you know, in any way a demand problem. The demand is there. This is very much a supply problem at the moment.

headline: Josh Gilbert notes Microsoft delivering huge profit numbers validating AI capital expenditure
reasoning: Microsoft is cited as one of the hyperscalers that reported strong earnings early in the season, demonstrating that AI capex is generating returns. This validates the investment thesis for continued AI infrastructure spending.
quote: We're also seeing it pay off from some of the names that we've already had reporting early in the earning season, right? Your Microsoft, your Amazons, your alphabets, delivering huge profit numbers from the outlay that they've already put out into AI. And I think that's the key part is that the outlay they're putting out is coming back through the door.

headline: Josh Gilbert characterises AI as still in its very early stages with the shift from 'thinking' to 'doing' (agents) set to exponentially increase compute demand
reasoning: Gilbert argues AI agents—systems that act autonomously rather than just responding to queries—will drive substantially more compute demand per task than current generative AI tools. This structural shift underpins continued capital expenditure by hyperscalers and sustained demand for AI infrastructure. He views current investment levels as only the tip of the iceberg and expects the cycle to continue rewarding AI infrastructure providers.
quote: The reason that demand keeps compounding is because of agents. And I think we're in the very, very early stages of AI... What we're seeing at the moment is we're really seeing this shift from the thinking to the doing stages... when you use an AI tool yourself, that's a query. But when an agent goes off and does it for you, that's very different. And ultimately, that's going to take a lot more compute... yes, we're seeing billions and billions of dollars invested, but we're only at the very tip of the iceberg here.

headline: Josh Gilbert says consumer staples stocks were rewarded in reporting season as a turnaround and recovery story

quote: On the other side, Consumer Staples were rewarded for what has been a bit of a turnaround and a recovery story in that sector. So overall, I think investors have been pretty pleased.

I guess really the interest is going to be what we hear around the conversation and maybe if we get any updates around this latest news and what that means for forecasts or maybe what it means for where rates are going to go from here.

headline: eToro's Josh Gilbert flags BOJ rate hike as the most important central bank decision of the week, with markets fully pricing a 25bp move to 30-year highs
reasoning: Gilbert highlights the Bank of Japan as the standout central bank event of the week, unlike the RBA and Fed which are expected to hold. Markets are fully pricing in a 25 basis point hike that would take Japanese rates to their highest level in over 30 years. He sees this as a double-edged sword: tightening poses risks for Japanese equities, but moving too slowly carries its own dangers. He also flags implications for the yen carry trade and notes Japanese stocks have performed strongly this year.
quote: The BOJ decision will be a really interesting one, because unlike the RBA and the Fed who are set to stay on hold, the BOJ looks at the high, high grades as well. Markets are fully pricing in a 25 basis point hike this week that would take the BOJ's rates to the highest level we've seen in over 30 years. So I think that's going to be a really important one to watch, you know, especially with, you know, the yen, you know, sort of a risk currency that a lot of investors have looked to over the years for that sort of carry trade as well.

headline: Josh Gilbert took a position in SpaceX IPO despite high valuation, arguing investors must think in decades not quarters with Musk-led companies
reasoning: Gilbert was initially skeptical of SpaceX given its $2.2 trillion valuation and lack of the cash flow positivity seen in other trillion-dollar companies. However, he concluded that with any Elon Musk company you are buying over decades rather than quarters, and that SpaceX is not just a rocket company but intertwined with AI. He notes bears betting against the Musk premium have been in a losing trade for the better part of a decade.
quote: You know, when you think of this company, the sort of the retail hype behind it, two point two trillion dollar valuation. There's only 15 companies on Earth that are worth over a fifth, you know, worth over a trillion dollars. And they're all long established cash flow positive. You know, SpaceX is neither of those things. So, look, I think with any Elon Musk company, you're buying over decades rather than quarters. And I think that's something really important to think about when investing in a company like this. You know, it's not just a rocket company. It's mixed in with many, many things, including A.I. So, you know, it's investors of always, you know, the bears, betting against Musk premium have been in a bit of a losing trade, let's say, for the better part of a decade. So I think it's hard to bet again, mystery on Musk.

headline: eToro's Josh Gilbert sees SpaceX IPO success and AI trade recovery as key tailwinds for tech and Asian markets, particularly the KOSPI
reasoning: Gilbert notes that a major overhang for markets had been uncertainty around the SpaceX IPO — whether it would strain liquidity or draw capital away from AI winners. The IPO going off without a hitch and finishing 90% higher removed that overhang. Combined with peace prospects reducing geopolitical risk, he sees a positive few days for the AI trade. He specifically highlights the KOSPI as a beneficiary, given most of its gains this year are AI-driven.
quote: I think a lot of pricing was we would see maybe a buckling IPO that wouldn't go. And I think that ultimately we saw a lot of good news coming from that SpaceX IPO. It sort of kind of went off without a hitch, obviously finished 90 percent higher. And then obviously this news coming out today, I think it's just been a positive few days for this sort of A.I. trade. And that's why we're seeing sort of, you know, Asian markets rallied today, especially something like the KOSPI, which is obviously seeing most of its gains this year coming from the A.I. trade.

headline: eToro's Josh Gilbert sees Bitcoin competing for risk capital against AI trade, with $60,000 a key technical level to watch
reasoning: Gilbert argues crypto's biggest challenge this year has been competing for risk capital with the AI trade, which has outperformed significantly. Bitcoin is down 50% from all-time highs, and new entrants like SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI offer similar 'generational technology' narratives but with actual balance sheets and cash flows. He does not think this capital diversion lasts forever and expects some rotation back into crypto eventually. He flags $60,000 as a critical technical support level — a break below signals further weakness.
quote: I think the biggest problem that we've seen for crypto this year is that it's really competing with a new sort of level of risk that it hasn't had to compete with for a few years. And that's coming from one, the AI trade that's obviously performed you know, outrageously well over the last sort of year or so... So I think it's just testing investors' priorities a little bit and where that sits. And I think that capital is just sort of directing elsewhere at the moment. I don't think it stays that way forever. I do think at some point we do see a bit of a rotation back in. You know, the prices are looking, you know, obviously much better value than where we have been in at other times. So I certainly think that's something to keep an eye on. $60,000 mark is a real key technical level for us that we're keeping eye on. Anything below that signals probably further weakness. If it can hold above that, then pretty positive moving forward.

headline: eToro's Josh Gilbert sees lower oil prices as a meaningful tailwind for equities and risk sentiment, reducing inflationary pressure and central bank uncertainty
reasoning: Gilbert argues that the prospect of peace in the Middle East removes a key source of geopolitical risk that has dominated market moves since February. Lower energy costs flowing through are seen as a meaningful tailwind for equities and risk sentiment. He also notes this reduces uncertainty around central bank policy, given inflation concerns linked to elevated energy prices. However, he cautions that details remain thin and headlines can turn quickly, urging investors not to chase the rally blindly.
quote: I think markets are obviously pricing in plenty of optimism at the moment, which I think is warranted given this sort of relief rally has been building for months now, if we think about how how long we've been talking about this conflict, how heavily it's dominated daily market moves since February. And I think ultimately it's not just sort of that, you know, the takeaway here of geopolitical risk is everything else, right? It's lower energy costs flowing through, which is obviously going to be a meaningful tailwind for equities, risk sentiment. When we think about, you know, the inflation concerns we've had recently in the US with the RBA hiking a number of times this year as well. So I think not only does it take that geopolitical risk off the table, it also takes off a level of uncertainty around what we've seen from, you know, central banks so far this year.

headline: SpaceX IPO success and peace prospects seen as positive catalysts for the AI tech trade globally

I think that's really hungover market because I think there was a lot of question marks over where the capital would flow from. You know, if it was going to strain liquidity, if it was going to come from some of those A.I. winners. And that's why I think, you know, mixed with, you know, the prospect of, you know, a rate hike from the Fed last week just obviously saw, you know, a lot of pressure coming onto that sort of A.I. tech trade. It sort of kind of went off without a hitch, obviously finished 90 percent higher.

headline: NVIDIA earnings this week are a high-stakes test for the entire AI trade, with constructive signals from AMD, Intel, TSMC and hyperscaler CapEx

If NVIDIA fails to raise the bar, the impact would extend beyond the stock to the entire AI sector and broader global equity markets including South Korea.
quote: I think the key thing here is if he doesn't, and we don't get that from NVIDIA, the market's really in a position that this isn't just NVIDIA that takes a hit, you know, it's the whole AI market as well as the broader market as well.

headline: Bitcoin holding around $80,000 in a relatively quiet period, with upside catalysts expected in back half of year from US regulation and corporate adoption
reasoning: Bitcoin has been unusually quiet during the current period of uncertainty, sitting around $80,000 after a drawdown from $120,000 at end of last year. ETF flows remain solid and the pro-crypto US administration and incoming regulatory changes are supportive. Gilbert expects activity to pick up in H2 as regulations make it easier for companies to hold Bitcoin on balance sheets, driving corporate allocation demand.
quote: I think that does start to change in the back end of the year, particularly when we see those regulations coming through and it being much easier for sort of companies to hold Bitcoin on balance sheets and things like that.

headline: Fed minutes mid-week are the key macro event as markets now price a 75% chance of a December rate hike
reasoning: Gilbert says Fed minutes will be scrutinised for signs the committee is shifting to a hawkish tone, or whether the bond market is getting ahead of itself. quote: Markets now pricing that December hike, I think 75% chance almost now of that December hike. So, I think really minutes are going to be scrutinized for any sign that we are really starting to see the committee shifting towards that sort of hawkish tone.

headline: US Q1 earnings growth of 27% — six consecutive quarters of double-digit growth — providing equity market support despite macro headwinds

Notably, companies have not been downgrading or lowering guidance on the back of the conflict, which Gilbert sees as a key standout positive for equity markets.
quote: Q1 earnings growth of over 27%, and that's the highest that we've had in years. It's a six straight quarter of double-digit growth, and obviously, tech is really leading the way.

headline: Bond market signalling inflation not yet beaten as prolonged Middle East conflict keeps oil elevated above $100
reasoning: Josh Gilbert argues the bond market is reacting to persistent inflation fears driven by Brent crude remaining above $100 for an extended period. The Middle East conflict has dragged on longer than analysts expected, with ceasefire hopes repeatedly dashed. This has shifted market pricing toward the Fed needing to hike rates in the back half of the year, a dramatic reversal from rate-cut expectations at the start of the year.
quote: The bond market is ultimately telling us that the market is worried about inflation, and it's not beaten yet. It's not beaten yet, and that's ultimately coming down to what we're seeing from oil prices.
